uncited: Spatial Indexing and Ordering encompasses the methods for mapping multi-dimensional volumetric data (typically 3D spatial coordinates, optionally combined with discrete dimensions like time) into linear memory structures to optimize spatial locality, cache coherence, and I/O efficiency.

It solves the problem of inefficient random access in dense grids by ensuring that spatially neighboring voxels are stored in adjacent memory locations, which is critical for high-performance volume rendering pipelines.
The family relies on the conversion of $N$-dimensional coordinates into a 1D linear index $I$ to facilitate storage in contiguous arrays.
**Arithmetic Strides (Row-Major):** Mapping coordinates $(i, j, k)$ to $I = i \cdot S_y + j \cdot S_z + k$, where $S_y$ and $S_z$ are strides derived from grid dimensions.
This provides $O(1)$ access but poor spatial locality for non-adjacent slices [S2, S4, unofficial].
**Space-Filling Curves (SFC):** Mapping coordinates using bit-interleaving (Morton/Z-order) or recursive curve traversal (Hilbert) to preserve locality.

The concept of mapping multi-dimensional data to linear memory for cache efficiency originated with the development of space-filling curves in mathematics and their subsequent application in computer graphics for data serialization and parallel processing.
